Note.Name: README
Note.Text:
## Overview

This repository contains the Forsta integration for Research Defender (RD). It
wraps both the client-side scripts that call the RD APIs and the server-side
logic that verifies responses and determines whether a respondent can continue
through the survey.

At a high level the integration:

- Collects RD Search V4 and RD Activity data into two Forsta text-list
  questions, `RD_Search` and `RD_Activity`.
- Validates and hashes RD Search data on the server before trusting the client
  payload.
- Retrieves RD Activity statistics server-side using an API token obtained in
  the browser.
- Aggregates the outcomes into a single-value question
  `research_defender_fail` where `0 = allow respondent to continue`,
  `1 = terminate respondent`.

## Configuration

The implementation is configured in the `consts` script. There are two steps
for configuration the project:

1. Fill in the `projectSettings` object (see comments for instructions)
2. Uncomment one of the template configs depending on the type of project.
   It is vital that this is set selected correctly because all of the termination
   logic depens on the values of this config. The defaults align with the company
   standard settings: 
   https://srcentre.sharepoint.com/:w:/s/AuditRiskandPrivacyCommittee/IQCcJahzDWdjRKFloXNC2qfeASJqFJQ_sPub2XwMWw4XtuQ?e=sUGs8X


## Data flow

1. Landing page (`client/onlineIntro.js`) unhides the intro content and the 
   next button only when RD calls finish. It listens for custom events fired by
   the producer scripts so the respondent cannot continue until responses are
   available.
2. **RD Search (`client/search.js`)** runs client-side, calls the RD Search V4
   endpoint, stores the raw payload and HTTP status into `RD_Search`, then fires
   the completion event.
3. **RD Activity token fetch (`client/activity.js`)** runs client-side, calls the
   RD Activity token endpoint, stores the raw token payload and HTTP status into
   `RD_Activity`, then fires its completion event.
4. **Server script (`rd.js`)** executes after the page submits. It parses and
   validates `RD_Search` via `processSearchResults()`, pulls statistics for
   `RD_Activity` via `processActivityResults()`, and finally computes
   `research_defender_fail` inside `determineOverallPassFail()`.

## Client-side behaviour

### search.js

- Uses `fetch` with credentials and an 8-second timeout supplied by Forsta macros
  (`^getTimeout()^`, `^makeRDSearchURL()^`).
- Writes `status_code` and `raw_response` to `RD_Search`.
- Emits a custom event (`^getSearchEventName()^`) so the intro screen can
  re-enable navigation.

### activity.js

- Calls the RD Activity token endpoint with the public API key. Response text
  goes into `RD_Activity.raw_token_response`, HTTP status into `status_code`.
- Emits a second custom event (`^getActivityEventName()^`) and unhides the intro
  once both events are received.

### onlineIntro.js

- Waits for both events (or detects prefilled hidden inputs) before restoring
  the original intro content and un-hiding buttons, preventing users from
  skipping the RD checks.

## Security considerations

The RD Search V4 endpoint supports signing the request URL with the private key
so Research Defender can confirm it was not tampered with. RD also signs the
response payload: `Validation.Surveys` and `Validation.Respondent` are hashes of
the corresponding entries in the `String` object. Because those string values are
not valid JSON, we extract key-value pairs via regular expressions to ensure the
data we trust matches what was signed. We should pursue a native, structured
response with RD to avoid depending on this workaround.

## HTTP status codes and timeouts

Both client scripts use an 8-second timeout. If a request does not complete in
time, it is aborted; the server interprets this as a failure since allowing the
respondent through would let malicious users block outbound traffic to bypass
screening. Every response captures the HTTP status code so we can differentiate
between network issues and valid RD denials.

FormText.Text:
Please wait ...

Thank you for helping with our survey.

We would like to remind you that there are no right or wrong answers - it's your own thoughts and opinions that matter. Any comments you make will not be linked to you personally, but will be reported as a group. Please take your time to complete the questionnaire thoroughly. For most questions, you will only need to click in a tick box with your mouse. Other questions will require you to type in a response or a value.

How to answer this survey:

  • Please read each question and follow the instructions to record your responses.
  • Please DO NOT use the 'Back' and 'Forward' buttons in the browser.
  • Please use the buttons at the bottom of each screen.
  • If you would like to pause the survey to return to it later, simply close the window and click on your original link to return.

FormText.Text:
Participant Information Sheet
Attitudes Towards Religious and Cultural Diversity Survey 2026
(Survey testing interview) 
Thank you for agreeing to take part in survey testing for the Attitudes Towards Religious and Cultural Diversity Survey. This information sheet will explain the purpose of the research and what is involved in a survey testing interview. In preparation for the interview, please read this Participant Information Sheet carefully, you will then be asked for your consent at the beginning of the interview.
Who is involved in the project? 
The Attitudes Towards Religious and Cultural Diversity Survey is being conducted by researchers from the Scanlon Foundation Research Institute and the Social Research Centre, with the Scanlon Foundation Research Institute leading the research.
The project is funded by the Australian Government through the Department of Home Affairs and was commissioned by the Office of the Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia.
Who is conducting the survey testing?
The Social Research Centre (http://www.srcentre.com.au), an independent Australian social research organisation, based in Melbourne and owned by the Australian National University (ANU) will carry out the survey testing. 
What is the research about?
The Attitudes Towards Religious and Cultural Diversity Survey is a national survey of how Australians think about religion, cultural diversity, and community life, including views and attitudes towards Muslims and Islam, and other religious and cultural groups. Results will be published in public reports and presented to government, community organisations, and the media.
Why is survey testing important?
Survey testing helps us understand how people interpret, understand and respond to questions. We want to know how easy the questions are to understand and how we can improve them. It also helps identify and correct any potential issues with the survey questions.
What is involved?
Testing of the survey will involve participating in an interview conducted either online via Zoom or Microsoft Teams or via telephone with a researcher from the Social Research Centre. Survey testing requires you to use a laptop or desktop computer (not your mobile phone). The interview will take up to 60 minutes.
At the beginning of the interview, you will be asked to consent to participate in the survey testing, and to confirm that you are happy to have the video and audio of the discussion recorded.
During the interview the researcher will ask you questions about how you interpret and understand the questions and whether any wording is confusing or could be improved. There are no right or wrong answers, the interviewer is interested in understanding how the questions are interpreted and whether they make sense. 
What are the benefits of taking part?
Participating in the survey testing means you will help shape the final survey questions for The Attitudes Towards Religious and Cultural Diversity Survey to make sure they are valid and fit for purpose in measuring views and attitudes towards religion, cultural diversity, and community life. This includes giving you the opportunity to tell us what you think about the questions based on your own experiences. Your feedback is important and will help identify potential issues with the questions, ensure the questions are being asked in the right way, and improve the overall survey experience for people.
As a thank you for participating in the survey testing interview you will receive an $80 eGift card upon completion of your interview.
Do I have to take part in this research?
This survey testing is voluntary, meaning you do not have to participate if you do not want to. You can change your mind at any time and say you no longer wish to be involved, even if you said yes at the start. Let the research team know if you no longer want to take part.  
What about my privacy?
All information you provide is confidential and will be used for research purposes only – this means your details will not be shared with anyone outside those working on the project at the Social Research Centre. Any information used in reporting will be anonymous or deidentified. Your personal information is protected by the Privacy Act 1988. 
With your permission, we will video, and audio record our discussion with you to assist in notetaking. We use this recording for analysis purposes only, making sure that your identity and confidentiality are protected at all times. We will remove any identifiable personal information (such as names or other identifying information) from our notes of the discussion before we begin analysis of the data. Audio-recordings and transcripts are stored securely and will be deleted in line with the Social Research Centre’s privacy policy and the Privacy Act 1988.
More information on the Privacy Policy can be found at https://srcentre.com.au/privacy-policy/. 
Are there risks in taking part?
The survey asks about general views and attitudes and is not intended to cause physical or emotional harm or intrude on your privacy. However, some questions cover topics that may feel personal, including religion, Muslims and Islam, other community groups, financial circumstances and political preferences. Some questions may also feel confronting, particularly if you are Muslim or have experienced prejudice. If any question or discussion topic makes you uncomfortable, you can choose not to answer it or end the interview at any time.
If you feel distressed or uncomfortable at any point, please seek support after the interview. You may wish to contact your GP or another health provider, or use one of the following free and confidential services:
•    Lifeline: 13 11 14
•    Beyond Blue: 1300 224 636
•    Suicide Call Back Service: 1300 659 467
•    13YARN (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander): 13 92 76
The following organisations also offer counselling and psychological support specifically for people from culturally diverse backgrounds:
State and Territory services:
•    NSW: Transcultural Mental Health Line: 1800 648 911
•    QLD: Queensland Transcultural Mental Health Centre: 13 74 68; World Wellness Group Multicultural Connect Line: 1300 079 020
•    VIC: Victorian Transcultural Mental Health: (03) 9231 3300
•    TAS: Migrant Resource Centre Tasmania: (03) 6221 0999
•    SA: STTARS (Survivors of Torture and Trauma Assistance and Rehabilitation Service): (08) 8206 8900; PEACE Multicultural Services: (08) 8245 8100
•    WA: ASeTTS (Association for Services to Torture and Trauma Survivors); (08) 9227 2700
•    NT: Melaleuca Australia: (08) 8985 3311; NT Mental Health Line: 1800 682 288
•    ACT: Companion House: (02) 6251 4550
Muslim community support:
•    Hayat Line: 1300 993 398 — a free, confidential crisis support line for Muslims in Australia, Monday to Friday 9am–5pm AEST.
•    Islamic Council of Victoria: (03) 9328 2067
What if I have further queries or concerns?
If you would like more information about this research project or to discuss any questions about participating, please reach out to Natasha Vickers at natasha.vickers@srcentre.com.au.
